Matt People’s

The version posted here would be cool on fiddle, but it’s a bit awkward on flute or whistle. Here’s a version for fluters.

X: 1
T: Matt People’s
M: 4/4
L: 1/8
R: reel
K: Ador
A2eA BAeA|B2gB BAGB|A2eA BAeA|1 BAGA BAAG:|2 BAGA BAAg||
ae~e2 agef|gB~B2 g2fg|ae~e2 aged|BAGA BAA2|
ae~e2 agef|gB~B2 g2fg|afge fded|BAGA BAAG||

This is the very first tune on the legendary recording “Molloy/Brady/Peoples,” and as many point out, it’s an easy substitute for a great fiddle tune Gravel Walks. Similar, but surprisingly easier.

Composer

↳ Posted by slainte on August 8th, 2004.

Matt Peoples’ reel composed by Siobhan Peoples?

In an interview published in spring 2004 in Fiddler Magazine
http://www.fiddle.com/issues/spr04.html#anchor1852610
Siobhan stated she was thirty-one years of age. This means she must be born around 1973.

Matt Peoples’ reels on Molloy/Brady/Peoples were recorded in February 1977. Well, I know some musicians start early …

Re: Matt Peoples’

Errigal is a conical mountain in Co. Donegal, formerly revered by the Fir Bolg, an ancient people.

↳ Posted by Jerry O'Donnell on December 14th, 2019.

Re: Matt Peoples’

On Siobhan Peoples as the composer of the two Matt Peoples tunes as further evidence, both tunes were published in Breathnach CRE2 (1976): in his tune notes it tells that both were obtained from Tommy Peoples, both in Dublin in 1968.

237. [Lady Doll Sinclair, Matt Peoples’s or Matt Molloy’s] Untitled from Tommy Peoples [fiddle], Dublin, III, 1968.

256. [Matt Peoples’s] Untitled from Tommy Peoples [fiddle], Dublin, III, 1968.

↳ Posted by JWiseman on December 1st, 2021.

Re: Matt Peoples’

Tommy Peoples wrote in his book that this tune, and possibly the one played with it in D, were learned by him from his uncle Mattha. Tommy never heard the tunes played by anyone else, and so called the set “Matt Peoples’ ” after their source, his uncle.

↳ Posted by Jerry O'Donnell on December 1st, 2021.

Re: Matt Peoples’

As stated above this tune is known in Scotland as “Lady Doll Sinclair”, first appearing under “Lady Doll St. Clair’s Reel” in J. Johnson Choice Collection of 1753, and 1758. It is also in Robert Bremner’s 1757 collection, and in James Oswald’s famous Caledonian Pocket Companion of 1760 as “The King of France”.

Again evidence of that extraordinary connection between Scotland and Donegal.
